author: buchanan_robert
text:
At first we thought it must be some beast or other,
Lying in the bushes and the grass below us,
But when they came up out of their hiding places

To take a good look at what had killed them all,
We knew that they were people like ourselves,

Only smaller—with heads like monkeys, hands like paws—

author: cushag
text:
We are not made to live alone, as men think we ought:—
It is the thought that makes us lone. And yet the stars
Above and the sea below shall never come within our reach,
For we who walk must ever be but shadows in their paths!

“No,” said I, “no, you are not going anywhere.”

She turned, and kissed me on the cheek again;

Her mouth smiled like the wind’s smile after rain—

It is as if I were listening for something,
Listening for the voice which used to speak to me,—

The light from a closed door in the middle distance,—
That is all that the memory will admit of:
But no one can find what has been lost forever.

author: buchanan_robert
text:
The little boy stood on the burning deck,
Whence all but him had fled;
The flame that lit the battlements
Was reflected in his eye.
He too might hide 'neath sheltering wing,
But nature cried aloud:
"Bold boy! be true to God and duty—
Stand for thy right or die!"
His hand shall ever hold a brand,
That never will grow dim;
For he who fights the hardest fight
Is champion worthy of the crown.

author: buchanan_robert
text: The dead men lie all night in their coffins, And the birds sit up late with their sorrow on them; For they know that soon from every corner Shall sound again the voice of gladness strong, With laughter ringing like a golden bell, That will ring through the silent street at dawn!

author: cushag
text:
I canna speak o' him as he deserve :
His manners were kind and his words were sweet ;
But there was one fault that did mar them both,
He would take the very last bit out of my bread.

author: emily_dickinson
text:
I wuz brought up to thort
That all young women should be chaste ;
And it turned out that so did you—
What could we do ?

"When it comes to gettin' clothes on ye,

Yer better not try her.

Her notions 'bout women's dress are all gone;

She thinks that everbody should be dressed up like her!"

author: cushag
text:
I've been tryin', ma missis, to teach my wife.
To make her mind what she should do ;
But when I tell her something that she must abide,
She thinks it ought to be noo.
It makes my life miserable — there ain't nobody
Will do like she says; and I have tried
In vain to teach her every thing from A down to Z—
And now you know, ma missus, why!

author: cushag
text: " If you ever goes up to Yorkshire," said old Mrs. Fetherstonhaugh, " and come near the town o' Leeds, stop a-while in the village o' Pudsey ; there ye shall find me living with my daughter 'at went from me when she was very young, and who has four or five children o' her own; and they do not take to drink nor get into bad company like folks in other places ; it would surprise one how good and innocent they are."

author: emily_dickinson
text:
I saw a lady who loved so much
 Her little dog that she'd kiss him goodnight;
 She never would let anyone touch him,
 Or else he’d run away and bite them right.

author: john_keats
text:
All the stars that shine at night
 Have been the lights of heaven,
 All the trees that bear sweet fruit,
 The flowers on summer lawn;
 All these were once as we are,
 In their beginning, too,
 But from our lives, O God!
 Take sorrowing them away.

You can not live in a cage
Without coming out at last;
But if you would not be defiled
Or stained with earth's foul dust,
Keep your wings folded away
As if you were not born.

author: emily_dickinson
text:
The wind was blowing hard that night,
 The rain it poured so fast,
 That a man might have walked out there
 Across the stormy blast;
 But I stood still for fear I'd drop
 My hand upon the glass
 Of an empty beer mug, which lay
 Upon the kitchen shelf;
 Then I dropped down again to bed
 For the next day would be sad,
 So no one could make me a drink
 In case they called for tea or bread.

And here is another:

I am going mad, - as every now and then the world must

author: emily_dickinson
text:
This was his love for her; a voice he heard,
 A sudden flush upon her cheek that came
 From an unknown wind or breeze which stirred
 Her spirit's flame in secret places there,
 Or from some subtle sense which spoke
 To him across a gulf whose depth he knew not.

author: john_keats
text: “I wonder what’s inside,” said Tom; “and I should like to see it.”

author: john_masefield
text:
I have a dog; you know how dogs bark,
How they beguile themselves on any task;
They chase their own shadow, play at balls,
Or drag about some straying bit of straw,
That might amuse them were it not for law;
Yet when I call my dog I find him there,
Sitting upon the table close beside me,
He knows where we are, what we eat or wear,
What our affairs are, where we have been,
The whole history of my life in a word,
So I am often led into absurd

As on my way I turned me towards the east,
To seek some refuge from my foes,
I heard the rustling of the leaves beneath,
Which told me well that they were near;
For while in vain I strove to find an end
Of these detested dangers sent;
By chance as I went out at sea's brink side,
A boat upon its course did glide.

The first is a sonnet. The second is not. In what ways do they differ? And why?

author: john_keats
text:
The kingly mind had many gifts,
But eloquence was one; and it's gift
Was like an orchard-tree whose fruit is bright
With golden apples; and its blossoms white,
As if the whole world were in blossom set.
To every thought there came a word that lit
It on fire; nor could one syllable be met
That did not kindle other syllables;
For all things seemed made for this man's delight.

author: john_keats
text: In this, which I am so happy as to call mine, I have been favoured in having the pleasure of seeing one who had never till then heard me read—a person to whom nothing could be more delightful than a well-chosen poem, but whose taste was too fine for what is commonly called poetry. The poems she has allowed herself to hear are few in number; not because they were very good or bad, but because her judgment is refined, delicate and critical.—She is one who knows every word of any poet, and would make you think there was not another being upon earth that had

author: john_masefield
text:
"His mother walked to meet him when he left school,
He had a job in London-town;
She thought that she might see him in his blue suit,
With stars upon his shoulders--all at once.
But now she walks along the dusty road,
To find a place for burial of her son."

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960

text:
"How can I tell my children that their Mother lies
In a cold grave under the rain?
That she who cared for them so long has now no care
Of any earthly thing?"

author: john_masefield
text:
"All day I go up-hill to the schoolhouse,
With a thousand thoughts in my head about
The lessons that I ought to learn there,
But it is hard for us poor folk to pay."

author: john_masefield
text:
"They said that I had been a clever fellow;
But in my day they never made any trouble."

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
All day long, my boat was out in sight of land,

But not one other ship appeared on the horizon.

I don’t mind being alone with the wind,

Nor do I mind the thunder-clouds breaking overhead;

But even when we came into harbor I felt lonely,

As if something had died within me which never came back to life again.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
You see, sir, my head is not so good as it
was; my back aches from carrying all this

Sea-water; my legs are weak with rheumatism;
my right hand shakes from weakness; and if I

Work much longer I shall go down in the hold.

I’m going down with him; not one moment longer

Will he live without me — Oh, this terrible weather!

Now here is my last will: take me away quickly, please!

For we are drifting now, as though in an ocean-current.

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
I see the white sails of my old ship
Under the yellow sun;

And how they flap against each other! . ..
But why do they wave so wildly? . ..

It is not wind in them, it is the call
Of an unknown land;

The home of an unknown race,
Wherein I am their brother!

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
‘My life is no longer my own’, the boy says,

As he lies in his bed, his heart all aching;

But one day I shall leave this earth below,

To sail with the clouds above upon high.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
“The ancient Romans, as they were men of great wisdom,
and lovers of philosophy, used to consider that nothing was
more necessary for man than an education; therefore their
fathers brought up their children after their own manner,
because they understood that it was more easy to teach them
to have good habits at first, than when grown to years.”

author: robert_frost
text:
The sun of love’s meridian shone bright upon her,
And made her youth to grow up in all its beauty;
Her cheeks were red like lilies, her eyes as blue as
the sky,
Her hair of brown like the honey from the hive of the
bee.

His food, when the ship lay in port at Syracuse, was such as only a beggar would have been allowed to eat; but while she rode in the open sea it had to be salt-fish, hard cheese, and dried figs; so that after three days' eating nothing else than these the sailors lost all their strength, and could not stand upright on deck without holding each other fast. And they were hungry even during this time.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
I am as poor as an oyster on the sands;

I'm as lean as a starved rat in a famine lands.

[10] A third piece of verse:

This old world is so like a stage whereon
All are players that ever come to town;
And their parts are assigned them by the Lord
To play upon this globe for which they were born.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:

him in prison?

With dried figs and olives only, as I remember.

He knows everybody, likes everybody,
And says he never meets a gentleman
Who doesn't know how to make a man feel at home.
We hear him telling tales about gentlemen,
Telling them down so nicely you don't want
To stop listening till they all are told out.
Well, sometimes we get tired of hearing
About rich people and their wives, and try
The odd old fellow in the corner next,
With the red waistcoat and the long pipe; but no,
Nothing ever

"We are not rich but we are free,
And this makes freedom very dear;
And life is lovely if you do
What you please, in spite of others who sneer."

author: robert_frost
text:
"The old man took no notice till the boy
Said something about his being in for all
That happened here, and if they should call in
Others. Then he said, "You must not do this,"
And bade them sit down; then added, "We shall know
What we are called on to support, as soon as
They're willing to explain how much they need."

author: robert_frost
text:
"The man's grown old in these seven years;
His face has lost its colour; wrinkles lie
Around the mouth and eyes as if they feared
They might not hold them long; but still he comes,
And all my pity for this poor boy grows
More intense. He never says more than,—
‘Mother! Will you give me something to eat?
Something —anything?’—but when she tells him no,
He goes away quite broken-hearted. Once
She gave him some cakes and tea. His cheeks grew bright
With joy and gratitude as he

author: stephen_crane
text:
I am a bird with wings,
With feathers I have grown;
The sky is my home, and there I go.
My nest is not made on high,
And yet it's a happy one for me,
For here I love to build my life.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
An old woman came walking down a path one day,
 Her eyes all full of tears and her heart was filled with pain.
 She sat down on a rock where she had never gone before,
 And there she sobbed for joy until her poor face became more red than any rose might be.
 The sun shone out so brightly over the earth below,
 That not even the grass could look at it without laughing low.
 It must have been something very wonderful indeed
 For such happiness as this which possessed an old woman's soul

I have not heard you sing this month;
 Where are your notes and keys?
 I thought you had them at home;
 But it is certain now!

This one is also known as 'The Three Little Birds':

There was once a little bird who sang so well,
 That every one called her Nightingale.
 She lived all alone, without any friends or neighbors,
 Until she met another bird just like herself.
 "If we join together," she said,
 "we shall be able to get some food."
 So they began to live together.

author: stephen_crane
text:
They are all gone out with the wind
 To seek for something far away;
 But I'm left here to think about you
 And sit and gaze at your pretty face-
 That is why I've not been able to fly.


The first poem seems more like an anti-war poem while the second one appears as an ode written in remembrance of someone who has died. The second poem does seem more romantic than the former but they both have the common theme of expressing love through poetry.

author: stephen_crane
text:
On a tree was seen, one day,
 The figure of a crow;
 Which had made its nest in a crevice,
 As well as could be done.

author: stothert_james_a
thomas_hardy
text:
Ourselves are all created from one light,
Which never can be changed or lost again.
We only now remember we have brought
This being up from night; and while so taught,

Can find no difference between creation,
Whatso'er may be made of us, or done :

The world's great heart beats; where my spirit hears
Its pulse from deep within me rise and fall—
That is my own dear country : there I find
What all desire beyond this narrow sphere.

author: stothert_james_a
text: The World a Dream of Beauty : I have seen The world a dream of beauty . . .

author: stothert_james_a
text:
Here Nature’s self was never seen,

Save where her power had long reigned,
Till she, within these hallowed scenes,
Drew Love, the soul of life and peace;
Nor, when this scene so well expressed
The sacred joy which oft comes at length
From prayerful seeking after rest
For wearied souls, or lonely thought :—

author: thomas_hardy
text:
I thought that God must love me very much
To give me such beauty and strength and grace
As I have had ever since He put His stamp
Upon my face, upon all things within range.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
A voice behind me called my name!
 I looked around to find it there,
 But saw only silence and the rain,

I WENT forth seeking knowledge,
And found only love:
One rose leaf was all my reward;
The price was too high!

I saw the morning twilight die
Beneath the western sea;
But never a pearl I found on its
brow, though I looked o’er it twice or three.

In vain did I seek beauty there,
For nothing is fair;
Beauty is not truth—or youth,
Or age, or strength, nor health, nor wealth.

Truth? Nay, the world knows naught but lies,
Since men are born

author: thomas_hardy
text:
I HAD never known what death could be
 Till I had felt it on my heart—
 Felt that cold finger on my soul,
 Which tells its coming very fast,
 Withal the sweetest thing apart!


Oh! how my spirit thrilled with awe,
 As slowly, gently, came the pain;
 The fear crept close upon me soon,
 But still my trembling lips were brave!
 Then was my mind with joy serene!

The world was dark, but then I saw
 One wondrous vision shining clear;
 All round my bed, within my sight,
 Lo!

author: thomas_hardy
text:
THE sun was sinking low.
 The last red rays went down!
 At once my heart grew slow.
 I heard some one around.
 Was it his voice? But soon
 My footsteps stopped. It ceased;
 For now all stillness seemed
 To speak within my breast.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
Here thou, great Anacreon! whose soul outstrangeth
 The girdle of the world, shall find a monument
 Where Angels wings their oars, or Phebus lamp
 Gives light divine, where Phoebus smiles in heaven,
 And leads his torches all along the sky.

author: buchanan_robert
text:
England for ever! when I see her green fields,
And hear her lambs bleat in some little fold,
 Or see those dewy meadows which lie brown
 And silent 'mid their furze-bushes covered o'er
 With dew, at early morn — the sun in showers
 Shines over them, and spreads his light abroad —

The Stars are all shining on my brow,
 And my heart glows with an inward glow.
 It may be for this I am so fair,
 Or perhaps because they have been here.
 To me the day is now but night,
 For which I thank them very much light.
 If they would only stay awhile,
 They could make all things look quite gay.
 Oh, how glad they must feel at seeing
 The earth looking so sweet as she is;
 How their spirits must soar when they view
 Her happy children all in merry mood;
 Oh! if they

author: william_wordsworth
text:
My country! in them is nothing sinister!
 No selfish faith or craftily-laid plan,
 To make their own secure at your expense stands
 Ajar behind the mask of public man;
 And though they play the hypocrites to please,
 They feel for you no false sentiment.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
My Country! in the hour of distance near,
 Oh, when she calls me back again,
 To joy in fruitful fields, or touch young springs
 With brightening feet, or hear, at eve,
 The peasant toil his household pleasures weave,
 So loved by God! And when in exile far,
 Where'er my dwelling, from my childhood's land,
 Or in my native valley's lonely glen,
 From hill to mountain, through green covert led,
